# What to Know About the Bricks & Minifigs Reckless Ben LEGO Scandal

Article by:
[Carolyn Hansen, J.D.](https://www.findlaw.com/company/our-team/carolyn-hansen-j-d/)

Contributing Author

Reviewed by
[Joseph Fawbush, Esq.](https://www.findlaw.com/company/our-team/joseph-fawbush-esq/)
|
Last updated on

[Follow us](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=https://www.findlaw.com/)

Over the last few months, a scandal has absolutely rocked families, Lego aficionados and anyone who loves justice. It’s the Bricks & Minifigs and Reckless Ben controversy — the subject of a viral YouTube investigation with millions of views. Here’s a breakdown of the LEGO scandal and the legal dispute that’s ensued.

## October 1999: Ed Mansell Started Collecting LEGO Star Wars Sets

In 1999, a man named Ed Mansell started collecting LEGO Star Wars sets. Over nearly two decades, his collection grew and grew. In the end, he had roughly 780 sealed LEGO Star Wars sets and around 1,200 rare minifigures. By 2023, his collection was described by some as the world’s largest LEGO Star Wars collection and was valued at up to $200,000 (although the actual value is disputed).

## Sometime in the Fall of 2023: Franchisees Purchased the Bricks & Minifigs Store

In 2023, a local Bricks & Minifigs (BAM) store had new franchise owners. Chrystal Law-Gorman and her husband Benjamin Gorman bought the Salem, Oregon, franchise of Bricks & Minifigs. Under the franchise model, franchisees pay royalties to the corporate entity. However, they remain fully responsible for daily operations, leases, and local banking. This is important because the Gormans later alleged that BAM Corporate failed to properly transfer key accounts and lease responsibilities to them. And BAM later alleged that the Gormans didn’t properly manage daily operations.

## September 2023: The Mansell Family Decided to Sell Ed’s LEGOs

By 2023, Ed was 83 years old and his health had declined. The family met and decided to sell his collection, and his son Bryan Mansell took the lead. Bryan was new to the LEGO resale world when he visited the Salem-Keizer, Oregon, BAM store. But his choice of BAM as a LEGO reseller was pretty reasonable because the store generally had a positive reputation as the most reliable and safest place to resell LEGOs. He even did a trial run with the store at the Rose City Comic Con, which was held September 22-24, 2023.

The Mansell family planned to use the proceeds from sales of the sets to fund higher education for Ed’s grandchildren. They had high hopes that the sale would go smoothly and that all the work that Ed had put into his collection over the years would pay off for the next generation.

## November 2023: Consignment Agreement Signed, and Mansells Started Receiving Payments

In November, Bryan was ready to act. He signed a contract with the BAM store owner Chrystal Law-Gorman and brought the LEGO Star Wars sets to her store. The contract said that he still owned the LEGO sets until they were sold on consignment. Like most consignment agreements, the store would take a percentage of the proceeds as payment.

At the time the consignment agreement was signed, Bryan said the LEGO collection was so extensive that it filled nearly all the shelves.

Throughout late 2023 and early 2024, Bryan received regular payments from BAM for sets that had been sold. He said that he received about $15,000. BAM corporate later alleged that their data showed more than $52,000 in sales during the same time period.

## November 2024: The Franchise Collapses and Corporate Steps In

On November 8, 2024, the Gormans informed BAM Corporate that the store was insolvent, citing nearly $200,000 in unpaid royalties, lease debts, and vendor obligations. Six days later, BAM Corporate removed the Gormans from the franchise and transferred control to two new franchisees — Brandon Best and Joshua Johnson.

The facts are disputed, of course, but the Mansell family alleges that their consignment inventory remained inside the building when Corporate transferred ownership. Chrystal reported that the new owners just walked in and forced her to leave. Security footage allegedly caught her telling Brandon that Bryan’s consignment inventory remained inside and did not belong to the store. What’s more, video evidence showed Brandon arriving at the store with a U-Haul truck, although this was later disputed.

Bandon and Josh’s account was different. They said that little Star Wars LEGO inventory was left in the store when they took possession. They claimed they had offered to return what little remained to Bryan, but he refused.

## Late 2024: The New Owners Said They Didn’t Know Anything About the Star Wars Sets

When Bryan arrived at the store in late November to collect payment, he claimed that the new owners denied knowing anything about the consignment agreement. Allegedly, they wouldn’t let Bryan look in the back for his items and threatened that any attempt at litigation would cost more in legal fees than the collection was worth. When Bryan called the local police, they refused to help —saying that the conflict was a civil matter and not a criminal one.

## 2025: Reckless Ben Starts an Investigation

Bryan was unsure what to do next. He [told his story on the Collecting Weekly podcast](https://open.spotify.com/episode/1Tuq8LHtlyvdacfjT0KTIS?si=L_j5EW63Tv-JIitHb9AKCw&nd=1&dlsi=4d1de5cb78234ed7) and also reached out to an independent documentary YouTuber named Benjamin Schneider, who is known online as Reckless Ben. Ben gathered records and tried to trace the missing assets. In April 2025, Ben even traveled to Utah to confront BAM’s corporate offices. Unfortunately, the encounter resulted in misdemeanor charges for trespassing and disorderly conduct.

## 2026: The Investigation Goes Public — Arrests, Online Chaos and Intensifying Legal Action

Reckless Ben eventually [published his investigation videos](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wscQpkcwgNU) on May 21, 2026, and the footage was so entertaining that it quickly went viral. Ben organized lottery-style raffles and even created a mock rival business called [We Steal From Old People](https://westealfromoldpeople.com/) with the tagline “If you’re old, we will definitely steal from you.” Millions of people became highly invested in the conflict.

In one incident, an actor dressed up as a UPS driver went to new BAM franchise owner Joshua Johnson’s house. Josh called the police. And the police arrested Reckless Ben on charges of stalking, trespassing, and targeted residential picketing. People online started making allegations about a conspiracy with a Mormon Mafia because Josh’s father held a senior position in The Latter-day Saints church.

Reckless Ben later claimed in his videos that he missed a court date and fled to Mexico around late March, asserting that a no‑bail warrant had been issued; Utah authorities have since said there was no active warrant for him at that time. However, the police have since contradicted his story, saying that there were no active warrants for him in Utah.

Also on March 27, Chrystal Gorman and her husband filed a lawsuit against BAM Corporate, alleging wrongful termination of the franchise agreement, wrongful seizure of store assets and inventory, breach of contract, fraud in the inducement, conversion and defamation.

## May 2026: BAM Corporate Takes Legal Action

Reckless Ben and the Gormans released some additional materials, too, which led to BAM Corporate filing a motion to compel arbitration and, on May 28, securing a temporary restraining order (TRO) and temporary injunction/gag order that limited public commentary about the matter.

They also filed a RICO lawsuit (under the federal [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act](https://www.findlaw.com/criminal/criminal-charges/racketeering-rico.html)) that named Reckless Ben, Bryan and others as part of an organized scheme of people who commit crimes such as threats and extortion. If BAM is successful, it could recover three times the damages it actually suffered.

Also in May, BAM submitted a formal complaint to Patreon requesting removal of Reckless Ben’s page and attaching the TRO and motion for a preliminary injunction. However, Patreon’s CEO Jack Conte released a public video siding with Bryan and Reckless Ben.

## June 2026: BAM Parts Ways With Brandon and Josh

By June 2026, things had not settled down in the least. It turned out that [police](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Dc368C7eWiY) [body-cam and dash-cam footage of Reckless Ben’s arrest](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Dc368C7eWiY), posted online by hackers, revealed inconsistencies between what viewers saw and the official reports. [Crowdfunding efforts](https://www.gofundme.com/f/help-bryan-recover-his-lego-collection) for Bryan had exceeded more than a half a million dollars. And BAM Corporate dissolved the Salem-Keizer franchise location altogether, cutting ties with Brandon and Josh completely.

In a [public statement](https://bricksandminifigs.com/blog/blog/2026/06/04/bricks-and-minifigs-salem-joshua-johnson-brandon-best-resignation/) released on Jun 4, 2026, BAM Corporate and CEO Ammon McNeff talked in detail about what they know, including that “Evidence shows there were three sets of books being managed by the previous owner Ms. Law/Gorman, regarding the collection, all with different accounts of what was sold and more reliable high-end market values for the entire collection, which is more accurately estimated at $95,000 to $100,000.”

On June 10, a Utah court upheld the TRO restricting Reckless Ben’s public statements, effectively silencing him. On June 11, an investigative Journalist called Coffeezilla published an [analysis of the financial records](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VKfQkRbd15k), which said that the LEGO Star Wars sets were never worth $200,000, and that the real value was, in fact, closer to $100,000.

A preliminary injunction hearing on June 30 resulted in removal of the matter to federal court, but the federal court has not yet ruled on the motion. The removal to federal court could affect the case in several ways. It will definitely affect the timeline, but it may affect the outcome too. Some attorneys believe that federal judges are better equipped to handle more complex commercial litigation and may apply procedural rules more predictably.

## July 2026: Legal Proceedings Continue

So, what’s next? There’s a lot going on. There’s the civil action between Reckless Ben and BAM. There’s the civil case against BAM by Chrystal Law-Gorman and her husband. Reckless Ben is also scheduled to attend hearings related to the criminal charges he faces. It’ll be interesting to see how it all plays out.

# FTC sues transgender care group, arguing it deceived parents and patients

The World Professional Association for Transgender Health has a leading role in determining how gender-affirming care is provided.

FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson said he's suing WPATH because it misled about the efficacy and safety of gender-affirming care. | AP

By [Simon J. Levien](https://www.politico.com/staff/simon-j-levien)

The Federal Trade Commission is suing the leading transgender health care group in federal court. The agency argued on Wednesday that the World Professional Association for Transgender Health made “deceptive claims” in its health care guidelines for transgender children. The group’s members include psychiatrists, surgeons, pediatricians, endocrinologists and primary care doctors who work with transgender patients.

The FTC, like the Health Department, has been on a monthslong legal tear to clamp down on providers and hospitals that offer gender-affirming care. Gender-affirming care refers to medical interventions for minors experiencing distress that their bodies do not align with their gender identity.

“Medical organizations must follow the science, disclose conflicts and put patients first,” said Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in a news release praising the FTC’s action.

The agency alleged that WPATH’s trans care recommendations violate the FTC Act by misleading parents and patients about the necessity and efficacy of these treatments. The FTC filed its [complaint](https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/WPATH-Complaint-Redacted.pdf) in the federal court in Fort Worth, Texas, alongside several red states, which joined the suit: Alaska, Iowa, Nebraska and Texas.

“The FTC filed a lawsuit against WPATH alleging that the organization made false and unsubstantiated claims regarding the necessity, effectiveness and safety of puberty blockers, hormones and sex-change surgeries,” said Andrew Ferguson, the FTC chair, in a news release. “Children, but especially their parents, must have complete and truthful information when making decisions to purchase medical services.”

Many of America’s leading provider groups, including the American Medical Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics, strongly support gender-affirming care. Providers have argued that transgender care can save children’s lives.

“The U.S. Federal Trade Commission is not a medical provider and has no place interfering with the process of individualized medical decision-making,” WPATH said in a statement. It said that the agency’s claims were “baseless.”

The Trump administration has pointed to a [British government review](https://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ukgwa/20250310143642/https://cass.independent-review.uk/) that found the evidence supporting gender-affirming care’s efficacy is weak, and [produced its own study](https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/hhs-releases-peer-reviewed-report-discrediting-pediatric-sex-rejecting-procedures.html) arguing the same. [The administration supported Tennessee’s defense](https://www.politico.com/news/2025/06/18/supreme-court-tennessee-transgender-care-ban-00411939) of its law barring gender-affirming care for minors in a Supreme Court case last year that Tennessee won 6-3.

The FTC probed WPATH alongside other physician organizations that drew up guidelines for gender-affirming care earlier this year. Then the provider groups — WPATH, the AAP and the Endocrine Society — sued the FTC, arguing in separate suits that the agency’s probe was retaliation and was a violation of their First Amendment rights.

Federal judges sided with the providers in the suits brought by WPATH and AAP, halting the FTC’s investigations. The Endocrine Society’s suit is still awaiting judgment.

KEIZER, Ore. (KATU) — An alleged consignment deal dispute at a Keizer franchise of the toy store Bricks and Minifigs sparked a national uproar online and is now the subject of numerous lawsuits.

It began as an alleged business arrangement between Bryan Mansell, the owner of a LEGO collection worth roughly $200,000, and Chrystal Law, the former franchise owner.

The controversy gained national attention after YouTuber Ben "Reckless Ben" Schneider published videos alleging that Bricks and Minifigs and its subsequent franchise owners improperly retained control of the collection after the store changed hands in late 2024.

The videos have garnered millions of views and sparked widespread discussion online.

## **Valuable LEGO Set Unaccounted For**

KATU spoke with Mansell on May 28th, but he declined to comment on the story.

Mansell and his father spent years building what they describe as a rare and valuable Star Wars LEGO collection worth roughly $200,000.

In 2023, Mansell entered into a consignment agreement with then-Keizer Bricks and Minifigs owner Chrystal Law.

**READ ALSO | [Portland teen designs LEGO's newest official set](https://katu.com/news/arc-pdx/grant-high-school-graduate-designs-lego-newest-official-set-toy-local-arc-italy-riviera-cool-fun-portland-oregon-teenager#)**

Under the agreement, the store would sell items from the collection and split the proceeds, while ownership of any unsold inventory would remain with Mansell.

The collection was publicly displayed at the store during a promotional event and was marketed as "one of the largest private Star Wars LEGO collections in the region" in a [social media post](https://www.instagram.com/p/CzXGqtBPby0/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA%3D%3D).

The arrangement allegedly continued until late 2024, when Bricks and Minifigs corporate says it terminated Law's franchise agreement and sold the store to the new franchise owner, Brandon Best.

## **What Is Alleged in the Video?**

In a [series of videos](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wscQpkcwgNU), Schneider alleges Bricks & Minifigs corporate and the franchise's new ownership knowingly took control of inventory belonging to the Mansell family when the Keizer store changed hands in November 2024.

He points to security camera footage in which Law is heard discussing unpaid consignment inventory during the transition and argues that company representatives were put on notice that the collection belonged to a third party.

Schneider further alleges the company later refused to allow Mansell to inspect inventory, provide a full accounting of the collection, or return items he claims remained unsold.

Schneider also argues that the collection was effectively converted into company-controlled inventory after the franchise takeover.

Throughout the videos, he alleges corporate officials, the incoming franchise owners, and others knew the collection existed, took possession of it, and either sold, transferred, or otherwise failed to account for a substantial portion of it.

The allegations have not been proven in court, and multiple lawsuits remain ongoing.

Bricks & Minifigs corporate announced Thursday that the Keizer location will be permanently closed. (KATU)

**Company Sues Over Alleged Harassment Campaign**

On May 27, Bricks and Minifigs, along with the current owners of the Salem-area franchise, filed a [lawsuit](file:///Users/vasilismac/Downloads/2026.05.28%20Verified%20Complaint%20(with%20Exhibits)(8986792.1)_SHarable.pdf) in Utah against Schneider, Mansell, and others.

The company alleges the defendants engaged in a coordinated campaign of defamation, harassment, trespassing, and extortion designed to pressure Bricks and Minifigs into paying money it did not owe.

In court filings, Bricks and Minifigs argues the dispute over the collection was a private agreement between Mansell and former franchise owner Chrystal Law that corporate leadership neither approved nor knew about.

The company alleges Law concealed details of the arrangement, underreported sales, underpaid Mansell, and left the franchise owing nearly $200,000 when she exited the business.

Bricks and Minifigs says it lawfully terminated the franchise agreement and found little Star Wars LEGO inventory remaining when it repossessed the store in November 2024.

In a news release on Thursday, the company announced that it is permanently closing its Keizer store and has mutually agreed to part ways with the Keizer franchise owners, Brandon Best and Joshua Johnson.

Best is also the owner of the Bricks &Minifigs franchise in Eugene.

The company said an internal investigation uncovered what it described as "significant evidence of gross negligence" involving both the store's previous operation under Law and recordkeeping issues during the ownership transition.

The company said the findings contributed to its decision to sever ties with the current franchise owners.

**READ ALSO | [Police bust massive Lego theft ring at Brick Builders in Eugene](https://katu.com/news/local/police-bust-massive-lego-theft-ring-at-brick-builders-in-eugene)**

According to the company, its investigation uncovered three separate sets of records related to the collection that allegedly contained discrepancies.

Bricks &Minifigs further claims that internal point-of-sale data show more than $52,000 in items from the collection were sold while the store was operated by Law.

The company said it has again reached out to Mansell and offered to review the records with him, return any inventory that can be identified as his, and compensate him for inventory that cannot be accounted for.

Bricks &Minifigs also said it is prepared to discuss removing Mansell from its lawsuit as part of a potential resolution.

"We continue our offer to sit down with you and are prepared to discuss dropping the lawsuit against you," said Bricks &Minifigs CEO Ammon McNeff in the statement. "Let's go through the spreadsheets and POS data together and ensure you are made whole monetarily."

## **Former Franchise Owner Challenges Company's Account**

Law and her husband, Benjamin Gorman, dispute Bricks and Minifigs' version of events.

In March, Law and her company filed a separate [lawsuit](file:///Users/vasilismac/Downloads/Item1_Complaint%20(2).pdf) against Bricks and Minifigs corporate, alleging the company wrongfully terminated the franchise agreement and improperly took control of the Salem-area store and its assets.

"In November 2024, our lives were turned upside down when the corporate franchisor behind our Bricks and Minifigs store in Keizer, Oregon, abruptly seized our business, changed the locks, confiscated our inventory, and publicly accused us of theft," said Law in a statement on GoFundMe. "After more than a year of trying to resolve this privately and professionally with corporate leadership, we were left with no choice but to file a lawsuit."

In an [online statement](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zedmOopRTm0), Law and Gorman alleged that Bricks and Minifigs corporate was aware of the consignment arrangement and acknowledged the collection when the store changed hands.

They also contend corporate representatives took control of the business, knowing inventory belonging to Mansell remained tied to the store.

Law and Gorman further allege that Bricks and Minifigs have attempted to shift responsibility for the dispute onto them while refusing to resolve the matter fairly.

They say they intend to continue pursuing their claims in court.

"We are disappointed that Bricks &Minifigs corporate continues to take steps that we believe are intended to delay the process and discourage us from speaking publicly," said Law.

An alleged consignment deal dispute at a Keizer franchise of the toy store Bricks and Minifigs sparked a national uproar online and is now the subject of numerous lawsuits. (FILE)

**YouTubers Arrested During Investigation**

As Schneider's investigation gained national attention, it also led to legal trouble in Utah, where Bricks and Minifigs is headquartered.

Schneider was arrested on March 11, 2026, after police accused him of repeatedly targeting the home of a Bricks &Minifigs employee and franchise owner while investigating the LEGO collection dispute.

Prosecutors later filed misdemeanor charges, including stalking, targeted residential picketing, criminal trespass, and disorderly conduct.

Police allege Schneider and others engaged in a pattern of conduct directed at company officials and their families.

Schneider has disputed those allegations, arguing in his videos that his actions were part of an effort to investigate what happened to the Mansell family's collection and to serve legal documents related to the dispute.

The criminal case in Utah remains separate from the ongoing civil lawsuits involving the Salem-area franchise and the disputed LEGO collection.

# Reddit fined £14.5m in UK over use of under-13s’ data

Information Commissioner’s Office imposes largest fine yet for a breach of children’s privacy

The UK information regulator has fined the social news service [Reddit](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/reddit) £14.5m for using the data of children under the age of 13 unlawfully and potentially exposing them to inappropriate and harmful content.

The hefty punishment from the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) is the largest fine yet for a breach of children’s privacy and comes after the US-based company introduced age checks in July, including age verification to access mature content. Prior to this, the ICO said, there were “a large number of children under 13 on the platform and Reddit did not have a lawful basis for processing their personal information”.

Reddit asks users to declare their age when opening an account but the ICO said relying on self-declaration presented risks to children as it was easy to bypass. The regulator also found Reddit failed to carry out a data protection impact assessment to assess and mitigate risks to children before January 2025.

“Children under 13 had their personal information collected and used in ways they could not understand, consent to or control,” said John Edwards, the information commissioner. “That left them potentially exposed to content they should not have seen. This is unacceptable and has resulted in today’s fine.”

It is the third largest financial punishment the ICO has issued, after a £20m fine for a British Airways data breach affecting more than 400,000 customers in 2018, and an £18.4m fine for the Marriott Hotel group when more than 300m customer records were affected in a 2014 attack.

Reddit said it would appeal against the decision. “The ICO’s insistence that we collect more private information on every UK user is counterintuitive and at odds with our strong belief in our users’ online privacy and safety,” a spokesperson said.

The company said it did not [require users](https://www.reddit.com/policies/privacy-policy) to share information about their identities, regardless of age, “because we are deeply committed to their privacy and safety”. It says it removes users under the age of 13 because they are not allowed. Its user agreement states that “by using the services, you state that you are [at least 13 years old”](https://support.reddithelp.com/hc/articles/360043066492).

Since last July, Reddit started requiring UK users who want to view mature content such as pornography to show they are over 18 by uploading a selfie or a photo of their government ID, in order to comply with the Online Safety Act.

Edwards said: “Companies operating online services likely to be accessed by children have a responsibility to protect those children by ensuring they’re not exposed to risks through the way their data is used. To do this, they need to be confident they know the age of their users and have appropriate, effective age assurance measures in place. Reddit failed to meet these expectations.”

# Post Office Escapes £1m Fine After Postmaster Data Breach

[News](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/)

## Written by

### [Phil Muncaster](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/profile/phil-muncaster/)

UK / EMEA News Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine

* [Email Phil](mailto:phil@pmmediauk.com?subject=Email from Infosecurity Magazine website)
* [Follow @philmuncaster](http://twitter.com/philmuncaster)

The Post Office has dodged a potential regulatory fine of over £1m ($1.3m) following a 2024 data breach in which it leaked the personal information of hundreds of postmasters litigating the company.

Data protection regulator the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) said in an update yesterday that the names, home addresses and postmaster status of 502 people were made publicly accessible from April 25 to June 19 2024.

The information was made available in an unredacted version of a legal settlement document on its corporate website, related to the notorious Horizon IT scandal.

Widely considered the biggest miscarriage of justice in British legal history, over 900 sub-postmasters were prosecuted for false accounting and theft, when in fact the problem lay with the Horizon IT systems the Post Office was using. Many served prison sentences or suffered bankruptcy as a result.

[*Read more on ICO public sector approach: Most UK GDPR Enforcement Actions Targeted Public Sector in 2024.*](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/uk-gdpr-enforcement-public-sector/)

 The ICO claimed that it considered a fine of just under £1.1m for the data breach, but didn’t think that the infringements reached the threshold of “egregious” under its public sector approach.

[That approach](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/ico-public-sector-fines/), which has been criticized in the past, posits that fines aren’t an effective deterrent in the public sector and only serve to further undermine the UK’s creaking public services. The Post Office is a limited company wholly owned by the government.

As a result, the Post Office has received only a reprimand from the ICO. That’s despite it failing to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect people’s information.

The ICO added that the company lacked documented policies or quality assurance processes for publishing documents on its corporate website, and that staff training was insufficient.

## Lessons Learned

The ICO did acknowledge that the Post Office offered compensation to all those impacted by the breach, as well as identity protection services for 24 months. It also contacted search engines to remove cached versions of the document.

The Post Office established an emergency working group for improving internal controls, and produced a documented policy for publishing information on its corporate website, the ICO added.

The regulator said organizations should learn the following from the incident:

* Have a clear protocol for publication of sensitive documents online, including multi-step approvals
* Ensure all teams recognize personal information, and can assess its sensitivity and potential reputational/emotional impact if published
* Centralize and classify documents using secure, shared repositories with clear access controls and classification labels, rather than personal storage like OneDrive
* Ensure everyone involved in publishing content understands their role and responsibility
* Deliver personalized training to relevant teams covering publishing protocols, data classification, and risk awareness

# Hauling with a higher purpose

How FTC Transportation balances a social mission with sharp fleet logistics.

[Seth Skydel](/21169200)

July 28, 2026

4 min read

[Add Us On Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=fleetowner.com)

## Key takeaways

* FTC Transportation uses a balanced freight strategy to support its mission while reducing empty miles and costs.
* Motive safety technology helps FTC Transportation coach drivers and improve fleet safety performance.
* The carrier’s driver-focused culture has earned recognition through Best Fleets to Drive For and TCA Elite Fleet programs.

In an industry defined by demand for carrying capacity, [FTC Transportation](https://www.ftctransportation.com/) stands apart with a purpose that extends beyond freight. Based in Oklahoma City, the carrier operates as a wholly owned subsidiary of Feed the Children. Across every mile it travels, the company’s mission is to help address child hunger across the U.S.

## FTC Transportation balances charitable freight with commercial operations

Founded in 1986, FTC Transportation is a full-service truckload operation that hauls donated goods and products purchased through charitable contributions to three [Feed the Children](https://www.feedthechildren.org/) warehouses. There, goods are sorted and distributed throughout communities nationwide.

FTC Transportation has a balanced freight strategy in addition to its role as Feed the Children’s core carrier, explained Emory Mills, SVP of FTC Transportation.

“Our No. 1 priority is to position capacity to meet Feed the Children’s needs,” Mills explained. “To minimize empty miles and help keep costs in check, we also leverage backhaul opportunities on the spot market by hauling dedicated freight and brokered loads for customers nationwide.”

FTC Transportation operates a fleet of approximately 25 company-owned tractors, primarily driven by solo operators, and is supported by a trailer pool of around 60 dry vans. Trailers are strategically staged at donor locations to improve efficiency and reduce delays in pickup and delivery.

Equipment purchasing at FTC Transportation typically involves soliciting bids for new tractors and trailers, often through long-standing partnerships with manufacturers such as Freightliner and, more recently, Kenworth. Over the past few years, the fleet’s appearance has evolved, with tractors now sporting a fresh green color scheme that reflects a more vibrant brand identity.

Supporting equipment operations at FTC Transportation is a centralized maintenance program. The company operates a full-service shop staffed by three full-time technicians who handle its internal fleet needs and provide light repair services for outside carriers. Mills noted that the in-house capability not only improves reliability but also reinforces the company’s commitment to safety and operational excellence.

[## How Ploger defeats compounding risk](/operations/article/55377920/how-ploger-transportation-uses-technology-and-disciplined-hiring-to-reduce-fleet-risk)

July 1, 2026

[## Inside Arka Express’ safety-first fleet strategy](/operations/article/55364305/arka-express-boosts-fleet-safety-with-ai-coaching-and-routing-tech)

May 5, 2026

## Safety technology and driver programs strengthen fleet performance

Safety, a cornerstone of FTC Transportation’s culture, is also reflected in the technology that has transformed how the company manages driver performance.

“Two years ago, we implemented [Motive](https://gomotive.com/) forward-facing dash cameras and electronic logging devices,” Julia Williams, safety and driver manager, said. “The cameras changed the game with in-cab coaching, helping to reduce and eliminate unsafe driving events like following too closely, stop sign violations, hard braking, and speeding.”

The Motive system captures video clips of safety-related events, giving FTC Transportation a clear view of real-world situations. These insights not only allow for more effective coaching, Williams noted, but also provide context when incidents are incorrectly flagged.

“Sometimes we can dismiss the issue if the driver is not at fault,” she added. “Overall, it gives us an opportunity to make improvements.”

According to Williams, “the technology has also increased driver awareness and uncovered behaviors that previously went unnoticed. It shows us some things we didn’t know were happening and makes our drivers more aware of the driving practices.”

The benefits extend beyond operations. Improved safety performance at FTC Transportation, for example, has strengthened relationships with insurance underwriters, potentially resulting in reduced premiums at renewal.

FTC Transportation’s commitment to its drivers has earned the company significant industry recognition. This year, the carrier was named a [Best Fleets to Drive For](https://www.bestfleetstodrivefor.com/) honoree for the 14th consecutive year and celebrated its fifth year in the program’s Hall of Fame.

A new milestone was also receiving the Best Fleets to Drive For Hall of Fame Stratosphere Award, an achievement typically associated with much larger carriers. The recognition reflects consistent excellence in driver satisfaction, workplace culture, and operational performance.

FTC Transportation was also designated a [TCA Elite Fleet](https://www.tcaelitefleet.com/), a newer program developed in collaboration with the University of Denver. Based on driver surveys and comprehensive evaluation criteria, Williams said the program provides valuable feedback while boosting morale across the organization.

“FTC Transportation exists to provide safe and reliable transportation resources with a dedication to operational service excellence while helping those in need,” Mills said. “That dual mission of commercial viability and social responsibility shapes our business approach. We’re not just moving freight. We’re ensuring that essential goods reach families and children who depend on them.”

As a trucking company that is more than a carrier, FTC Transportation is proving that success is measured not solely by miles or revenue, but by the difference those miles make.

## Coupang hires US law firm for data breach lawsuit

South Korean ecommerce firm Coupang has hired the US law firm [Kirkland & Ellis](https://www.kirkland.com/) to represent it in a damages lawsuit filed in the US District Court for the Eastern District of New York.

The lawsuit, submitted by SJKP earlier this month, seeks US$5 million in damages over a data breach affecting 33 million customers in Korea.

SJKP alleges Coupang failed to adequately protect personal data and misallocated security funds, and it seeks to hold senior executives at Coupang’s US headquarters accountable for decisions related to security policies and incident response.

Over 7,000 individuals are reported to have joined the case.

The legal move comes amid increased regulatory scrutiny of Coupang in Korea and tensions between Seoul and Washington.

*🔗 Source: [The Korea Herald](https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10680469)*

## 🧠 Food for thought

Implications, context, and why it matters.

### A dispute over numbers is fueling a broader cross-border conflict

* The US damages lawsuit sits inside a wider fight. Large American investors are also pursuing investor–state dispute settlement (ISDS) arbitration, a process that lets foreign investors bring claims against governments, under the U.S.-Korea Free Trade Agreement against the South Korean government [1](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/more-u-investors-sue-south-165632607.html).
* Those investors say the government treated Coupang unfairly. They cite a threatened fine cap of up to 3% of revenue, which they argue could top $800 million for Coupang, and they compare it with other breach cases they say drew smaller penalties [1](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/more-u-investors-sue-south-165632607.html).
* The core argument centers on how much data was exposed.
* The Korean government’s joint investigation said private information from more than 33 million customers was exposed. It also said delivery address and order-list pages were viewed more than 1.48 billion times, including about 50,474 views of a page with unencrypted shared entrance door passwords [2](https://cm.asiae.co.kr/en/article/2026021109340354219).
* Coupang and its investors counter that the employee kept data from about 3,000 accounts. They argue the government is overstating the damage [1](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/more-u-investors-sue-south-165632607.html).

### One company’s failure is reshaping an entire nation’s tech policy

* Officials are using the breach as a reason to rewrite rules for South Korea’s platform economy [3](https://koreatechdesk.com/korea-platform-regulation-post-coupang-startup-impact-2026).
* Lawmakers are moving toward requirements that push platforms to build safeguards into daily operations, instead of relying on penalties after violations [3](https://koreatechdesk.com/korea-platform-regulation-post-coupang-startup-impact-2026).
* Measures discussed in this debate, including the Online Platform Fairness Act, would require disclosure of exposure (ranking) criteria, which explains how platforms decide what appears more prominently, plus standardized settlement timelines [3](https://koreatechdesk.com/korea-platform-regulation-post-coupang-startup-impact-2026).
* These duties can weigh more heavily on smaller startups with fewer staff and tighter budgets, which can slow growth [3](https://koreatechdesk.com/korea-platform-regulation-post-coupang-startup-impact-2026).
